guides.title: Holy water
guides.sub: A reminder of baptism, at the church door and at home
what: Holy water is water blessed by a priest or deacon with the Church’s prayer. It is a sacramental: not a sacrament, but a sign the Church gives us which, by her prayer, prepares us to receive grace and disposes us to cooperate with it. The Catechism names the sprinkling of holy water as a sign “which recalls Baptism.”

That is its whole meaning. When you sign yourself with it at the church door, you remember that you were washed in Christ and belong to him, and you ask to be made clean again before you pray. “We are buried together with him by baptism into death,” says Saint Paul, “that, as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life.”
Christians have taken holy water home for well over a thousand years, to bless themselves, their families and their houses. Used with faith, it is a small daily renewal of the promises of baptism.

In the older rite the priest also blessed salt and mixed it into the water, recalling the prophet Elisha, who cast salt into the bad spring of Jericho and healed it. Blessed salt is a sacramental of the same kind as holy water, and means the same: a prayer for cleansing and protection, made in faith.
how: On entering a church, dip the fingers of your right hand in the font and make the Sign of the Cross, remembering your baptism.
At home, keep a small font by the door, or a bottle in a fitting place, and bless yourself as you go out and come in.
Many parents sign their children with it at bedtime or as they leave the house.
Sprinkle the room of someone who is ill, or the rooms of your home, with a short prayer such as the Our Father.
To obtain it, take some from your parish’s holy water container in a clean bottle kept only for it, or ask a priest or deacon to bless water you bring.
At Easter, water is blessed at the Vigil. Where your parish offers it, you may take some home.

When it is old or no longer clean, pour it onto the earth, in the garden or a plant pot, or ask the parish to pour it into the sacrarium, the sink in the sacristy that drains straight into the ground. Do not pour it down an ordinary sink or drain.
Clean a home font now and then, and pour the old water on the earth.
If you would like blessed salt, ask a priest.
not: Holy water is not a charm. The Catechism calls it superstition to credit sacred signs with power by their mere outward use, apart from the faith and dispositions they ask of us (2111).
It does not replace Baptism, confession or the Anointing of the Sick.
More is not better. One Sign of the Cross made with faith is enough.
Blessed things are treated with reverence and kept from profane use; but if a little is spilt, wipe it up and think no more of it.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1667 to 1670 and 2111
Code of Canon Law, canons 1166 to 1171
General Instruction of the Roman Missal, 280 and 334, on the sacrarium
Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), “Holy Water”, and (1912), “Salt”
Fr William Saunders, on disposing of blessed objects, Arlington Catholic Herald (2003)

guides.title: The Brown Scapular
guides.sub: Our Lady of Mount Carmel: a sign of belonging to Mary
what: The Brown Scapular is two small pieces of brown woollen cloth joined by cords and worn over the shoulders, one piece on the breast and one on the back. It is a reduced form of the habit of the Carmelite friars. The Church calls it “an external sign of the filial relationship” between Our Lady of Mount Carmel and those who entrust themselves to her protection, turn to her intercession, and keep in mind the primacy of the spiritual life and the need for prayer.

To wear it is to be clothed in the habit of Mary’s family. The rite of enrolment calls it a reminder that in Baptism we have been clothed in Christ. Pope Pius XII hoped that it would be, for those who wear it, a sign of their consecration to the Immaculate Heart of Mary.

Carmelite tradition holds that Our Lady gave the scapular to the Carmelite Saint Simon Stock in 1251, with the promise that whoever dies wearing it will not suffer eternal fire. The story is not found in the earliest sources, and the Church does not ask anyone to believe it. Rightly understood, the promise expresses trust in Mary’s help for those who live and die faithful to her Son. It is not a pledge that the cloth will save someone who refuses him.

A second tradition, the “Sabbatine privilege”, rests on a papal bull of 1322 which historians judge not to be genuine. In 1613 the Holy See allowed the Carmelites to preach only that the faithful may piously believe that Our Lady will help after death, especially on Saturdays, members who died in charity, having worn the habit, kept chastity according to their state, and said the Little Office of Our Lady (or kept certain fasts). No one is obliged to believe it, and the Carmelites no longer preach it; our hope rests on Christ’s mercy, which Mary asks for us.
how: Ask a priest to enrol you. Enrolment is a short rite, made once in a lifetime. The Church asks that it be prepared for and not improvised.
Wear it at all times, usually under your clothes.
When it wears out, replace it with another. A new scapular needs no new enrolment.
Since 1910 the Church has allowed those already enrolled to wear a blessed medal in place of the cloth. It shows the Sacred Heart of Jesus on one side and Our Lady on the other.
Let it remind you to pray each day, to go to Mass and the sacraments, and to imitate Mary’s humility, purity and prayer.
Burn or bury a worn-out scapular; do not throw it away.
not: It is not a guarantee of heaven for someone who chooses to live in grave sin. Without faith, conversion and the sacraments it means nothing, and to think otherwise is the superstition the Catechism warns against.
Wearing it is not an obligation. If you forget it or take it off for a while, there is no sin: put it back on.
Do not rely on promises of release from purgatory on a set day.
There are other scapulars, each tied to its own devotion; the five-fold scapular joins five of them on red bands. Ask a priest before taking one up, and do not multiply them.
from: Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001), 205
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1670 and 2111
Pope Pius XII, Neminem profecto latet
Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), “Scapular”

guides.title: The Miraculous Medal
guides.sub: Our Lady’s medal, and its prayer
what: In 1830, in the chapel of the Daughters of Charity in the rue du Bac in Paris, a young sister, Saint Catherine Labouré, saw Our Lady, who asked that a medal be struck. With the approval of the Archbishop of Paris the first medals were made in 1832, and it came to be called the Miraculous Medal.

On its face Mary stands on the globe, crushing the serpent, with rays of grace falling from her hands, and around her the prayer: “O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.” On the back are the letter M beneath a cross, the Hearts of Jesus and Mary, and twelve stars. The Church calls it a “Marian microcosm”: it recalls the Redemption, the love of the Sacred Heart and the sorrowing Heart of Mary, Mary’s part in her Son’s work, the Church, and the bond between heaven and earth.

Like other Marian medals, it is a witness of faith, a sign of reverence for the Mother of God, and of trust in her protection. Its heart is the short prayer round its edge: to turn to Mary often, as a child does.
how: Have it blessed by a priest or deacon.
Wear it, usually round the neck, or carry it with you.
When you see or touch it, say its prayer slowly: O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.
No enrolment is needed to wear it.
Its feast, kept by the Vincentian family, is 27 November.
not: The Church says it is “never to be regarded as a talisman,” or to lead to any blind credulity.

The promise of great graces to those who wear it asks, in the Church’s words, for a humble and tenacious commitment to the Christian message, faithful and persevering prayer, and a good Christian life.
It is not more powerful for being larger, dearer, or worn in a particular way.
Do not pass it on with chain-letter promises or threats.
from: Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001), 206
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1670 and 2111
Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), “Miraculous Medal”

guides.title: The Saint Benedict Medal
guides.sub: The cross of Saint Benedict, against the tempter
what: Saint Gregory the Great tells how Saint Benedict trusted in the cross of Christ and worked wonders by its sign. The medal that bears his name shows on its face the saint holding a cross and his Rule, with the words “May we be strengthened by his presence at our death.” On the back is a cross covered with initials of short Latin prayers.

On the cross: C S S M L, Crux sacra sit mihi lux, “May the holy cross be my light”; and N D S M D, Non draco sit mihi dux, “Let not the dragon be my guide.” In the angles: C S P B, Crux Sancti Patris Benedicti, “The cross of our holy father Benedict.” Around the edge: V R S N S M V S M Q L I V B, Vade retro, Satana; nunquam suade mihi vana. Sunt mala quae libas; ipse venena bibas: “Begone, Satan; never urge vain things upon me. What thou offerest is evil; drink thine own poison.” Above the cross is PAX, peace, or the name of Jesus.

The meaning of the letters was recovered in 1647 at the Abbey of Metten in Bavaria, from a manuscript of 1415. Pope Benedict XIV approved the medal in 1741 and 1742. The design most often seen today is the jubilee medal first struck in 1880 for the fourteen hundredth anniversary of the saint’s birth.
The medal is a prayer in metal: a choice of the cross over the tempter, and a request for a good death.
how: Have it blessed by a priest. Its traditional blessing is a short exorcism; since 1964 any priest may give it without a special faculty.
Wear it or carry it, or keep it at home, in the car or at work.
Pray its words, in Latin or English, when you are tempted, and its prayer for a good death.
Let it turn you to the cross: to confession, to prayer, to resisting the first movement of temptation.
not: It is not a lucky charm and has no power of its own. Its strength is the cross of Christ and the faith of the one who prays.

It does not replace confession, or a priest’s help where real spiritual trouble is feared. Illness, especially of the mind, is to be distinguished from the action of the evil one and is a matter for medicine (Catechism, 1673).
Do not use it to frighten others or to curse anyone.
from: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), “Medal of Saint Benedict”
The Medal or Cross of Saint Benedict (The Liturgical Press, Collegeville, 1980)
Saint Gregory the Great, Dialogues, book II
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1673 and 2111

guides.title: Blessed objects
what: The Church blesses things as well as people: rosaries, crucifixes, medals, images, candles. Every blessing praises God and asks his gifts for those who will use what is blessed, and sets it apart for a holy purpose.

Like all sacramentals, blessed things do not give grace as the sacraments do. In the Catechism’s words, “by the Church’s prayer, they prepare us to receive grace and dispose us to cooperate with it” (1670). The Second Vatican Council says there is hardly any proper use of material things which cannot be directed to the sanctification of people and the praise of God.

A blessed rosary does not pray better than an unblessed one. What the blessing adds is the Church’s prayer, joined to yours whenever you use it. Devotions and the things that serve them should flow from the liturgy and lead back to it; they are helps, not the centre.
how: Ask a priest or deacon to bless them. Any priest may bless religious articles, and deacons may bless rosaries and many others. Lay people may lead certain blessings, such as those of the family, but they do not bless religious articles.
One blessing is enough. Ask again only if you are unsure that a thing was ever blessed.
Keep blessed things in a fitting place, and never put them to a profane use.
Lending a blessed rosary to someone does not undo its blessing.
Using a blessed crucifix, rosary, scapular or medal with devotion carries a partial indulgence.
When a blessed object is broken beyond use or worn out, do not throw it in the rubbish. Burn it, or bury it in the earth; broken rosaries and statues are usually buried. Your parish can help.
Do not sell a thing for its blessing: spiritual things can be neither bought nor sold (Catechism, 2121). You may freely give it away.
not: A blessing does not make a thing powerful in itself. To trust in the object rather than in God is superstition (Catechism, 2111).
A thing need not be blessed to be prayed with: an unblessed rosary is still a rosary.
Do not gather blessed things for their own sake. One crucifix that is looked at is worth more than many that are not.
If a blessed thing is lost, or thrown away by mistake, there is no sin in it.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1667 to 1679, especially 1670, 1671 and 1675; and 2111 and 2121
Second Vatican Council, Sacrosanctum Concilium, 13, 60 and 61
Code of Canon Law, canons 1166 to 1171
Book of Blessings (1989), General Introduction and the order for blessing rosaries
Pope Paul VI, Indulgentiarum Doctrina (1967), norm 17
Fr William Saunders, on disposing of blessed objects, Arlington Catholic Herald (2003)

guides.title: Relics
guides.sub: Honouring the saints through what they left behind
what: A relic is something a saint has left us: part of the body, something the saint used or wore, or a cloth or other object that has touched the saint’s tomb or remains. Catholics commonly call these first-, second- and third-class relics.

Relics are venerated, never worshipped: worship belongs to God alone. As the Catechism says of holy images, the honour passes beyond the thing to the person it brings to mind; here, to the saint, and through the saint to God, whose grace made the saint holy.

Scripture tells of a dead man who came to life when his body touched the bones of Elisha, and of cloths that had touched Saint Paul being carried to the sick, who were healed. The bodies of the saints were temples of the Holy Spirit and will rise again; the Council of Trent asked the faithful to honour them, and to keep the veneration free of superstition and of all trade.
how: Before a relic, pause and pray. Ask the saint to pray for you, and thank God for the saint’s life. If the reliquary is offered to be kissed, you may kiss it.
Keep a relic at home in a fitting place, not as an ornament or a curiosity.
If you inherit a relic, keep it with reverence, with any certificate of authenticity that came with it. If you cannot care for it, give it to your parish or diocese.
Never sell a relic. The Church absolutely forbids it (canon 1190), and a relic is not part of an estate to be valued.
If you see relics offered for sale, do not trade in them; you may let your diocese know.
Major relics, and those the people greatly venerate, may not be given away or moved for good without the permission of the Holy See.
not: A relic is not a charm, and nearness to it is not a measure of grace.
Only those the Church has beatified or canonised may be honoured with public veneration (canon 1187), and the public veneration of relics is under the bishop’s care.

The Church’s authentication of a relic is a careful human judgement, not a matter of faith. Treasure relics that come with a bishop’s or a religious order’s certificate, and be wary of relics of unknown origin. Be wary of relics of unknown origin.
from: Code of Canon Law, canons 1186, 1187 and 1190
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1674 and 2132
Council of Trent, session 25, on relics (as given in the Catholic Encyclopedia)
Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), “Relics”

guides.title: The Sign of the Cross, genuflecting and bowing
what: Christians have signed themselves with the cross from the earliest centuries. Tertullian, writing early in the third century, says that at every going in and coming out, at table, in lighting the lamps, in lying down and sitting down, “we mark our foreheads with the sign of the cross.”

The Catechism says that the Christian begins the day, prayers and activities with the Sign of the Cross, dedicating the day to the glory of God, and that the sign strengthens us in temptations and difficulties. It is a creed in a gesture: the cross by which we are saved, and the name of the Trinity into which we were baptised.

A genuflection, bending the right knee to the ground, is a sign of adoration, and so it is kept for Christ in the Blessed Sacrament (and for the Holy Cross from Good Friday until the Easter Vigil). A bow is a sign of reverence and honour. Made slowly and with attention, these gestures bring the heart with them.
how: Make the Sign of the Cross with the right hand, from forehead to breast, then from the left shoulder to the right, saying: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
Make it on waking, before and after prayer and meals, at the start of work, before sleep, and in temptation.

On entering and leaving a church where the Blessed Sacrament is kept, genuflect towards the tabernacle: the right knee touches the floor, the body stays upright. Whoever passes before the Blessed Sacrament genuflects, unless walking in a procession.
If age or illness makes genuflecting hard, bow instead. God asks for the heart, not the knee.
At Mass, bow your head when the three divine Persons are named together, and at the names of Jesus, of Mary, and of the saint in whose honour the Mass is celebrated.
Bow your head before you receive Holy Communion.
not: Do not hurry it. A Sign of the Cross made carelessly says little; made slowly, it is a prayer.
These gestures are not magic, and leaving one out through distraction is nothing to worry about.
A genuflection is for the Lord present. When the tabernacle is empty, a bow to the altar is enough.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1378 and 2157
General Instruction of the Roman Missal, 160, 274 and 275
Tertullian, De Corona, chapter 3
Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), “Sign of the Cross”

guides.title: Receiving Holy Communion well
what: In Holy Communion we receive Christ himself. Saint Paul warns that whoever receives unworthily, “not discerning the body of the Lord,” eats judgement to himself; so the Church asks us to prepare, and to receive with faith.

What matters most is within: faith that it is the Lord, love, and a heart made clean. The outward things the Church asks, the fast, a bow, the Amen, are there to serve that. The Catechism asks that our bearing “convey the respect, solemnity, and joy of this moment when Christ becomes our guest.”

Anyone conscious of grave sin must go to confession before receiving. If there is a grave reason to receive and no chance to confess, one must make an act of perfect contrition, which includes the resolve to confess as soon as possible (canon 916).
The Church asks us to receive at least once a year, at Easter time if possible, and encourages us to receive on Sundays and feast days, or even daily, when we are rightly disposed.
how: Fast from food and drink for at least one hour before Communion (not before Mass). Water and medicine do not break the fast. The elderly, the sick, and those who care for them are excused from it (canon 919).
If you have committed a grave sin, go to confession first.
Bow your head before you receive.
When the minister says “The Body of Christ,” answer “Amen,” and mean it.
You may receive on the tongue or in the hand, as you choose. In the United States Communion is received standing, but anyone who wishes may kneel.

On the tongue: open your mouth, put out your tongue a little, and keep still. In the hand: hold your hands open, one beneath the other, and put the host in your mouth there and then, before the minister, before you step aside. Look for any fragment in your palm.
You may receive a second time on the same day only at a Mass in which you take part (canon 917).
Afterwards, stay a few minutes in thanksgiving if you can.
When you cannot receive, make a spiritual communion: tell the Lord you desire him, and ask him to come into your heart.
not: Communion is not a reward for the perfect. If you are not sure whether a sin was grave, ask your confessor and follow his advice.
Not going up is not a public statement. No one need receive because others do; stay in your place and make a spiritual communion, without embarrassment.
If you realise that you have broken the fast, do not receive at this Mass; you may receive at a later Mass once the hour has passed, or on another day. It is not a sin to have forgotten.
Do not hurry away. A minute of silence after receiving is worth more than many words.
from: Code of Canon Law, canons 916, 917 and 919
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1385 to 1389
General Instruction of the Roman Missal, 160 and 161
Redemptionis Sacramentum (2004), 90 to 92
United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, “Worthy Reception of Holy Communion” (2011)

guides.title: Blessing your home
guides.sub: The Epiphany chalk, a priest’s blessing, the Sacred Heart
what: A Christian home is meant to be a small church: a place where God is welcome and prayer is natural. Blessing it asks God to dwell there and to keep all who live in it, and reminds them whose house it is. When Christ entered the house of Zacchaeus he said, “This day is salvation come to this house.”

At the Epiphany many families bless their homes, writing over the door in chalk the year and the letters C, M and B, joined by crosses: in 2027, 20 + C + M + B + 27. The letters are usually read as the initials of Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, the names tradition gives the Magi, and as Christus mansionem benedicat, “May Christ bless this house.” The Magi entered the house and found the child with his mother; we ask that he be found in ours.

The household can do this itself, led by a parent; the bishops of the United States publish an Epiphany blessing of the home for households to use. A priest or deacon can bless a house at any time, and it is good to ask when moving into a new one. Some families also enthrone an image of the Sacred Heart in the home, as a sign that Christ is its king; that devotion has its own guide.
how: On or near the Epiphany, gather the household at the main door.
Read the Gospel of the Magi or of Zacchaeus, say the Our Father, and ask God’s blessing in your own words or with a prayer such as “Visit, we beseech thee.”
Write the inscription above the door with chalk; if your parish blesses chalk at the Epiphany, use that.
Go through the rooms with holy water if you have it, praying for those who live and work there.
Ask your parish priest to bless your home, especially a new one.
Keep a crucifix in a central place, and pray together there.
not: A blessing is not a protection spell, and the inscription is a prayer, not a seal against harm.
It is not required. A home that has not been blessed is not cursed or unprotected in God’s eyes.
Nothing is gained by repeating the blessing again and again. Renewing it each year is the custom.
from: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, “Blessing of the Home and Household on Epiphany”
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1669 and 1671

guides.title: Parents blessing their children
guides.sub: A cross on the forehead, and a prayer
what: Parents have always blessed their children. Jacob blessed the sons of Joseph; the priests of Israel blessed the people with words still used today: “The Lord bless thee, and keep thee.” Our Lord took the children in his arms, laid his hands on them and blessed them.

Every baptised person is called to be a blessing and to bless (Catechism, 1669). The blessings closest to the Church’s sacramental life are kept for priests and deacons, but lay people may give others. The Book of Blessings grounds these in the priesthood that belongs to all the baptised, and its order for blessing sons and daughters allows the parents themselves to trace the sign of the cross on their children’s foreheads.
A parent’s blessing is not a priest’s blessing, and does not need to be. It is a father or mother asking God, with the authority of love, to keep a child they cannot always keep themselves.
how: Trace a small cross on the child’s forehead with your thumb and say: May God bless you, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Or use the old blessing from the Book of Numbers.
Do it at bedtime, when they leave the house, before a journey or an examination, on birthdays and on the anniversary of their baptism.
Use holy water if you like.
Grown children can be blessed too, if they are willing, and they may ask for it.
not: It is not a sacrament, and it does not take the place of Baptism, confession or a priest’s blessing.
It does not have to be done perfectly or every night. A missed night means nothing.
There is no need to copy a priest’s gesture of blessing with a raised hand; the cross traced on the forehead is the custom the Book of Blessings itself gives parents.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1669
Book of Blessings (1989), General Introduction, 18, and the Order for the Blessing of Sons and Daughters, 174 to 194
United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, “Sacramentals (Blessings)”

guides.title: Candles, palms and ashes
guides.sub: Candlemas, Saint Blase, Palm Sunday, Ash Wednesday
what: Some sacramentals belong to particular days and take their meaning from them. On 2 February, the Presentation of the Lord, the Church blesses candles and carries them in procession, remembering Simeon, who took the child in his arms and called him “a light to the revelation of the Gentiles.” The day was long called Candlemas. Candles kept in the home are a sign of Christ, the light of the world, and an expression of faith.

On 3 February, the memorial of Saint Blase (Blaise), bishop and martyr, throats are blessed with two candles blessed the day before, crossed and held to the throat, asking that through his intercession we be kept from illness of the throat and from every other harm.
On Palm Sunday blessed palms are carried in procession to welcome Christ as king. Kept at home, they are a witness to faith in him.

On Ash Wednesday ashes, made by burning the palms of the year before, are placed on our heads with the words “Repent and believe the gospel,” or “Remember, man, that thou art dust, and unto dust thou shalt return.” They begin Lent, a season of conversion: “Rend your hearts, and not your garments,” says the prophet Joel.
how: Bring candles to Mass on 2 February to be blessed, or take one home. Light it at family prayer, in time of trouble, or beside someone who is sick or dying.
Have your throat blessed on Saint Blase’s day, or when your parish offers it. It may be given by a priest, a deacon or a lay minister, and may be brought to the sick at home.
Keep your palm behind a crucifix or holy picture. Before Lent, return it to your parish if the parish gathers palms to burn for ashes; otherwise burn it or bury it.
Receive ashes on Ash Wednesday with a resolution for Lent. There is no rule about how long to leave them on.
not: Palms are not to be kept as amulets, or for healing or magical reasons, to drive away evil spirits (Directory on Popular Piety, 139). The same is true of candles and ashes.
Ashes are a sacramental, not a sacrament: they do not forgive sins, as confession does. Receiving them is a custom the Church warmly encourages, not an obligation.
Ashes are a sign of repentance, so they are for sinners, which is all of us. The Church’s blessings may be given even to catechumens and to those who are not Catholics (canon 1170).
The blessing of throats is a prayer, not a cure; it does not replace a doctor.
from: Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001), 123 and 139
Book of Blessings (1989), Order for the Blessing of Throats on the Feast of Saint Blase, 1624 to 1655
Code of Canon Law, canon 1170
Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), “Ash Wednesday”

guides.title: Asking for a Mass to be offered
guides.sub: For someone living or dead, for a need, in thanksgiving
what: Every Mass is the one sacrifice of Christ, offered for the whole Church and the world. A priest may also offer a Mass for a particular intention, and canon law says he may offer it for anyone, living or dead (canon 901). It is the greatest thing we can do for those we love.

Judas Maccabeus sent an offering to Jerusalem for sacrifice to be offered for the dead, “thinking well and religiously concerning the resurrection.” The Church has offered the Eucharistic sacrifice for the dead from the beginning.

It is the custom to give an offering, sometimes called a stipend. The Mass is not bought: spiritual things can be neither bought nor sold (Catechism, 2121), and the Church forbids even the appearance of trading in Masses (canon 947). The offering is a gift to the Church and helps support its priests (canon 946). Priests are urged to celebrate for the intentions of the poor even when no offering is given (canon 945).
how: Ask at your parish office, in person, by telephone, or online if the parish allows it. Give the person’s name, say whether they are living or dead, and mention a date if it matters, such as an anniversary.
Give the offering your diocese suggests. If you cannot afford it, ask anyway.

Each offering accepted has its own Mass (canon 948). If your parish cannot offer it soon, the intention may be passed to other priests, often missionaries; it must be offered within the year (canons 953 and 955).
Go to that Mass if you can, and pray there for the person.
Mass cards are best obtained from a parish or a religious house, so that you know a priest stands behind them.
not: The offering does not buy grace. A Mass said for a poor person who could give nothing is no less a Mass.
Do not have Masses said out of anxiety, as if salvation were a sum to be paid. Give what you can, and trust the rest to God’s mercy.
from: Code of Canon Law, canons 901 and 945 to 958
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1032, 2121 and 2122
Irish Catholic Bishops’ Conference, Canon Law regarding Mass Offerings (2010)
Diocese of Kilmore, Frequently asked questions about Mass cards

guides.title: The Anointing of the Sick, and calling a priest
what: The Anointing of the Sick is a sacrament for those in danger from illness or old age. It “is not a sacrament for those only who are at the point of death” (Catechism, 1514). Saint James writes: “Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” The prayer of faith, he says, will save the sick man, the Lord will raise him up, and his sins will be forgiven.

It may be received by any Catholic who has reached the use of reason and begins to be in danger through sickness or old age; before a serious operation; by the elderly as they grow frail; and again if the illness grows worse, or if a new serious illness comes. Only a priest can give it.

At the end of life the Church gives Holy Communion as Viaticum, food for the journey, and the priest can give the apostolic pardon, a plenary indulgence for the hour of death. If no priest can come, the Church herself grants that indulgence to a dying person who is rightly disposed and has been in the habit of praying during life; the use of a crucifix is recommended.
Do not wait. Many people die without the sacraments because the priest was called too late. Calling him does not mean giving up hope, and the sacrament brings peace.
how: Call your parish when someone is seriously ill, before surgery, or when an elderly person is failing. Ask for the Anointing of the Sick and, if possible, for confession and Communion.

At night or in an emergency, call the parish number; many parishes give an emergency line on their answering message. In hospital, ask the staff for the Catholic chaplain or the priest on call. Say plainly that someone is in danger of death and needs a priest.
If you can, prepare a small table with a crucifix, a candle and holy water.

If the person is unconscious, call the priest anyway. The sacrament is given to those who would have asked for it (canon 1006), and if there is doubt whether a person has died, the priest may still anoint (canon 1005).
If death has come before the priest arrives, call him even so; he will pray with you for the one who has died.

At the bedside, stay close and pray aloud, slowly: the Hail Mary, the Our Father, short prayers such as “Jesus, Mary and Joseph” and “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.” Help the dying person make an act of sorrow and of trust. Hold a crucifix where they can see it. Speak words of love and forgiveness, even if they seem not to hear.
not: It is not only the “last rites.” It is for the seriously ill, not only for the dying.
It is not for minor ailments, and it is not given to the dead.
Past sins are no reason to hold back: the sacrament is for sinners, with confession if possible. It is refused only to those who obstinately persist in manifest grave sin (canon 1007).

Do not blame yourself if someone you love died before a priest came. God’s mercy is not limited to the moment the priest arrives, and the Church grants her indulgence to the dying even when no priest is there.
from: Code of Canon Law, canons 921, 922 and 998 to 1007
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1514 to 1516
Apostolic Penitentiary, Decree of 19 March 2020, citing the Enchiridion of Indulgences, 12
Fr Daren Zehnle, “Who Can Receive the Anointing of the Sick?”, Catholic Times, Diocese of Springfield in Illinois

guides.title: Praying for the dead
guides.sub: Purgatory, November, and the holy souls
what: Those who die in God’s grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are assured of their eternal salvation; after death they undergo purification, so as to reach the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven. The Church calls this final purification purgatory. It is entirely different from the punishment of the damned (Catechism, 1030 to 1031).

Because the living and the dead are one family in Christ, we can help them. From the earliest days the Church has honoured the memory of the dead and offered prayers for them, above all the Eucharistic sacrifice; she also commends almsgiving, indulgences and works of penance on their behalf (Catechism, 1032). Scripture calls it “a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead.”

The Catechism adds that our prayer for them is capable not only of helping them, but also of making their intercession for us effective (958). Many Catholics therefore also ask the holy souls to pray for them.
On All Souls’ Day, 2 November, the Church remembers all the faithful departed, and November has long been kept as their month.
how: Have Mass offered for them, especially on anniversaries.
Pray for them by name. “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord” is short enough for every day; Psalm 130, “Out of the depths,” is the Church’s old prayer for the dead.
Visit their graves, especially in November. Pray there, tend them, and remember.
Offer for them a work of mercy, a sacrifice, or an indulgence you gain.
Remember the forgotten dead, for whom no one prays.
If you wish, ask them to pray for you.
not: Do not assume that someone is already in heaven and so stop praying for them. The Church declares a person a saint only after careful inquiry, and prayer offered for one already with God is never lost.
Do not despair of anyone either, after a hard death or a life far from God. We do not know what passed between the soul and God at the end; leave the judgement to him, and keep praying.
Purgatory is not a second chance for those who rejected God, nor a lesser hell. It is the last work of mercy that makes us able to see God.
Be wary of promises that a certain prayer said so many times frees a set number of souls, or frees them on a given day. The Church gives no such guarantees; God alone knows the state of each soul.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 958, 1030 to 1032 and 2111
Saint John Chrysostom, as quoted in the Catechism, 1032
Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), “Months, Special Devotions for”

guides.title: Holy hours and visits to the Blessed Sacrament
guides.sub: Time with the Lord in the tabernacle
what: Christ is truly present in the Blessed Sacrament, and the Church has always offered him adoration, not only during Mass but outside it, keeping the consecrated hosts with care and exposing them for solemn veneration (Catechism, 1378). “To visit the Blessed Sacrament is ... a proof of gratitude, an expression of love, and a duty of adoration toward Christ our Lord” (Catechism, 1418, quoting Pope Paul VI).

A holy hour answers the Lord’s question in the garden: “Could you not watch one hour with me?” It need not be an hour. A visit of a few minutes on the way home is a true visit. “Jesus awaits us in this sacrament of love” (Catechism, 1380).
What to do there is simple: be with him. Pray, read Scripture slowly, say the Rosary, speak to him in your own words, or be silent and look at him.
how: Genuflect on entering and on leaving. When the Sacrament is exposed in the monstrance, kneel for a while if you can, then sit.
Begin by placing yourself in his presence; an act of faith in your own words is enough.
If it helps, follow a simple pattern: adore, thank, ask pardon, ask, and then simply stay.
Read a passage of the Gospel slowly, such as John 6 or the Last Supper discourse.
Find out when your church is open, and when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed. If you take a regular hour of adoration and cannot keep it, tell those who arrange it rather than feel guilty.
not: It is not a test of endurance. Do not measure it by the clock or by your feelings.
Distractions are not failure. Each time you notice one, come back gently.
Do not fill the time with prayers to get through. Our Lord warned against much speaking; leave room for silence.
It does not replace Mass. Adoration flows from the Mass and leads back to it.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1378, 1380 and 1418
Pope Paul VI, Mysterium Fidei (1965), 66, as quoted in the Catechism
General Instruction of the Roman Missal, 274

guides.title: Consecration
guides.sub: Giving oneself wholly to Christ, through Mary or with Saint Joseph
what: To consecrate oneself is to give oneself to God without reserve. We were first given to him in Baptism, when we were buried with Christ and rose to walk in newness of life. Every later act of consecration is a deliberate yes to what Baptism began, and a renewal of the promises made then.

Consecration to Jesus through Mary, consecration to the Sacred Heart, and entrustment to Saint Joseph have one aim: to belong more completely to Christ. Mary and Joseph do not take his place; they lead to him, as Mary said at Cana: “Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.”

A consecration is not a single act that does its work and is finished. It is a way of living: offering each day, praying, receiving the sacraments, and turning to Mary or Joseph as to a mother or father.
how: Prepare for it with prayer and reading, often over some weeks, and choose a feast day on which to make it.
Make it freely, and ask a priest’s advice if you are unsure.
Renew it simply: each morning with a short prayer, or once a year on the day you made it.
A set preparation, such as the thirty-three days before a consecration to Jesus through Mary, can be kept day by day under Novenas, with your own intention.
not: It adds no burden under pain of sin. If you forget to renew it, simply begin again.
It is not a guarantee, and it is not a programme to be completed perfectly.
It does not put Mary or Joseph in God’s place.
One consecration that is lived is better than many made and forgotten.
from: Saint Paul, Letter to the Romans, chapters 6 and 12

guides.title: The Angelus
guides.sub: Morning, noon and evening; the Regina Caeli at Easter
what: The Angelus recalls the moment the Word became flesh: the angel’s message, Mary’s yes, and the Incarnation. Said morning, noon and evening, it lets the mystery at the heart of the faith mark the hours of an ordinary day.
In many places a church bell is still rung for it, and people stop what they are doing to pray. From Easter to Pentecost the Regina Caeli takes its place, rejoicing in the Resurrection.
It takes a minute. Its value is in the stopping: a short turning of the heart to God in the middle of work.
how: Say it early in the morning, at noon, and in the evening; or once a day, at noon, if that is all you can do.
If you hear an Angelus bell, pause and pray.
It was traditionally said kneeling, but standing on Sundays and on Saturday evenings; the Regina Caeli is said standing.
Say the versicles slowly, letting each bring the scene to mind: the angel, Mary’s answer, the Word made flesh.
not: It is not a duty, and the hours are not exact. Said a little late, it is still the Angelus.
One Angelus said with attention is better than three said in haste.
from: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), “Angelus”
Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), “Regina Coeli”

guides.title: Grace, churches and passing sirens
what: Some of the simplest Catholic customs are prayers tied to ordinary moments. None of them is a rule of the Church. They are ways of remembering God through the day, as Saint Paul asks: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God.”

Grace before and after meals is the oldest of them. Our Lord looked up to heaven and blessed the loaves before he broke them, and Moses told the people that when they had eaten and were full they should bless the Lord.

Many Catholics make the Sign of the Cross when they pass a church, greeting Christ present in the tabernacle; many say a short prayer when they hear an ambulance or see a funeral go by. These are popular customs, good and simple, not obligations.
how: Before meals, make the Sign of the Cross and say grace, at home and, quietly, in public.
After meals, give thanks, and remember the dead, as the old grace does.
Passing a church, make the Sign of the Cross or bow your head, and greet the Lord: “O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine.”
When you are driving, keep the gesture in your heart and your hands on the wheel.
When you hear a siren, pray for the person in need and for those helping them: a Hail Mary, or “Lord, have mercy.”
When a funeral passes, say: Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.
not: These customs are not obligations, and forgetting them is not a sin.
They are not charms against accidents or bad luck.
Do not make a show of them, and do not be ashamed of them.
from: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2157

about: When God forgives a sin, its guilt is taken away and our friendship with him is restored. But every sin, even a small one, also leaves something behind: a disordered attachment to created things that still has to be healed, either in this life or after death in purgatory. The Church calls this the temporal punishment due to sin. She is careful to say that it is not God taking revenge from outside; it follows from what sin does to us, and a conversion that comes from fervent love can heal it entirely.

An indulgence is a remission before God of some or all of that temporal punishment, for sins whose guilt has already been forgiven. The Church grants it, on conditions she sets, from what she calls her treasury. That treasury is not money or goods. It is the boundless worth before the Father of Christ’s merits, together with the prayers and good works of Our Lady and the saints, shared among all who belong to the communion of saints.
An indulgence is partial when it removes part of that punishment and plenary when it removes all of it. You may gain it for yourself or offer it for the dead.

The Church’s purpose is not only to lessen a debt. She wants to draw us to prayer, penance and works of charity. Pope Paul VI wrote that indulgences cannot be gained without a sincere change of heart and union with God, and that the Mass, the sacraments and works of charity always come first. No one is obliged to gain an indulgence. They are offered as a help.

For that reason the four general grants matter most for daily life. They attach an indulgence not to a set prayer or place but to the turning of the heart in an ordinary day: lifting the mind to God at work, serving someone in need, giving something up for love of him, and quietly bearing witness to the faith.
norms: Anyone who is baptised and not excommunicated can gain an indulgence, provided they are in the state of grace at least by the time the work is finished.
You need at least a general intention of gaining indulgences; you do not have to name each one. Some people make this intention once a day, for instance in the morning offering.
The work must be done at the time and in the way the grant describes.
A plenary indulgence can be gained only once a day. A partial indulgence can be gained many times a day.
At the hour of death a plenary indulgence can be gained even if one has already been gained that day.
You may gain an indulgence for yourself or offer it for the dead. It cannot be applied to another person still living.
When an indulgence belongs to a particular day and asks for a visit to a church, the visit may be made from noon on the day before until midnight at the end of the day itself.
If a feast is lawfully moved to another day, its indulgence moves with it.

A work you are already bound to do, such as Sunday Mass, does not carry an indulgence unless the grant says so. But if the penance given you in confession is itself an indulgenced work, doing it can serve for both.
Indulgenced prayers may be said in any language, in an approved translation. It is enough to say them alternately with someone else, or to follow them in your mind while another says them.
If illness or another real obstacle keeps you from the work or the conditions, a confessor can change them for you.

plenaryConditions.title: The work itself.
plenaryConditions.text: Do the prayer, visit or good work to which the Church has attached the indulgence, at the time and in the way she describes.

plenaryConditions.title: Sacramental confession.
plenaryConditions.text: Make a good confession within several days before or after the work. The Apostolic Penitentiary, explaining this rule in 2000, spoke of about twenty days. One confession can serve for several plenary indulgences.

plenaryConditions.title: Holy Communion.
plenaryConditions.text: Receive Communion within the same span of days, preferably at Mass and, if you can, on the day of the work itself. Each plenary indulgence needs its own Communion.

plenaryConditions.title: Prayer for the Pope’s intentions.
plenaryConditions.text: One Our Father and one Hail Mary for the intentions of the Holy Father are enough, though you may choose any other prayer. This too is said once for each plenary indulgence, fittingly on the day of the work.

plenaryConditions.title: No attachment to any sin.
plenaryConditions.text: You must turn your will away from every sin, even venial sin. This concerns what you want, not what you feel: a sincere will to have no sin at all is what is asked. If this detachment is not complete, the indulgence is still partial.

indulgences.partialNote: A partial indulgence asks less: do the work with a contrite heart, in the state of grace. Confession, Communion and the prayer for the Pope are not needed each time. To the good that the act itself already does, the Church adds an equal remission from her treasury, so the love and sorrow you bring are what count. If you set out to gain a plenary indulgence and something is missing, a condition or full detachment from sin, the indulgence is partial rather than lost. And if a work such as the Rosary is cut short for a good reason, the part you prayed carries a partial indulgence.

generalGrants.title: Lifting the heart to God in the day’s work.
generalGrants.text: While you carry out your duties and bear the hardships of life, you raise your mind to God with humble trust and add a short prayer, even only in your mind. Each such moment carries a partial indulgence. The Church adds that whoever turns to God like this through many moments of the day receives more grace and, in charity, can help the souls in purgatory all the more.

generalGrants.title: Serving those in need.
generalGrants.text: Led by faith and with a merciful heart, you give yourself or your goods to serve brothers and sisters in need. This carries a partial indulgence.

generalGrants.title: Giving something up.
generalGrants.text: In a spirit of penance, you freely go without something lawful that you enjoy. This carries a partial indulgence. It is a chosen, hidden penance in an ordinary day, not one laid on you.

generalGrants.title: Bearing witness to the faith.
generalGrants.text: In the particular circumstances of daily life, you freely and openly bear witness to your faith before others. This carries a partial indulgence.

grants.title: Consecration of a family
grants.work: A family consecrates itself to the Sacred Heart of Jesus or to the Holy Family of Jesus, Mary and Joseph, saying an approved prayer of consecration together before an image of the Sacred Heart or of the Holy Family, with a priest or deacon leading if possible.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the day the family first makes its consecration, for each member who takes part.
grants.partialWhen: On the anniversary of the consecration.

grants.title: Act of dedication to Christ the King
grants.work: Saying the act of dedication of the human race to Jesus Christ the King, which begins in Latin “Iesu dulcissime, Redemptor” (“Most sweet Jesus, Redeemer”).
grants.plenaryWhen: On the solemnity of Christ the King, when the act is said publicly, for example with the parish.
grants.partialWhen: At other times, or when said privately.

grants.title: Act of reparation to the Sacred Heart
grants.work: Saying the act of reparation to the Sacred Heart, which also begins in Latin “Iesu dulcissime” (“Most sweet Jesus”).
grants.plenaryWhen: On the solemnity of the Sacred Heart, when the act is said publicly.
grants.partialWhen: At other times, or when said privately.

grants.title: The papal blessing Urbi et Orbi
grants.work: Receiving with devotion the blessing the Pope gives to the city of Rome and to the world (Urbi et Orbi), or the papal blessing that a diocesan bishop is permitted to give to his people.
grants.plenaryWhen: When you receive the blessing in person or, if you have a good reason not to be there, follow it live by television or radio with a devout intention.

grants.title: Days set apart for the whole Church
grants.work: Taking part with devotion in the celebrations of a day the Church keeps everywhere for a religious purpose, such as praying for vocations to the priesthood and religious life, caring for the sick, or strengthening the young in faith.
grants.plenaryWhen: When you take part in the celebrations held for such a day.
grants.partialWhen: When you pray for the intention of such a day.

grants.title: Teaching or learning the faith
grants.work: Giving time to teaching Christian doctrine or to learning it.
grants.partialWhen: Whenever you teach or study the faith.

grants.title: Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament
grants.work: Visiting Our Lord in the Blessed Sacrament to adore him, whether exposed or in the tabernacle, or addressing to him an approved prayer such as the Adoro te devote, O sacrum convivium or Tantum ergo.
grants.plenaryWhen: On any day, when you spend at least half an hour in adoration.
grants.partialWhen: For a shorter visit, or for an approved prayer to Our Lord in the Blessed Sacrament.

links.label: A visit to the Blessed Sacrament

grants.title: Tantum ergo on Holy Thursday
grants.work: Joining devoutly in the Tantum ergo as the Blessed Sacrament is carried to the altar of repose after the evening Mass of the Lord’s Supper.
grants.plenaryWhen: On Holy Thursday, at the solemn transfer of the Blessed Sacrament after the Mass of the Lord’s Supper.

grants.title: A Eucharistic procession
grants.work: Taking part devoutly in a solemn procession of the Blessed Sacrament, inside a church or outside it, or in the solemn Eucharistic rite that closes a Eucharistic congress.
grants.plenaryWhen: Above all on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ, and at any solemn Eucharistic procession.

grants.title: First Holy Communion
grants.work: Receiving Holy Communion for the first time, or being present with devotion at a first Communion.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the day of a first Communion, for the one who receives and for those who devoutly attend.

grants.title: Prayer before a crucifix after Communion
grants.work: After Communion, before an image of Christ crucified, saying devoutly the prayer “Behold, O kind and most sweet Jesus” (En ego, o bone et dulcissime Iesu).
grants.plenaryWhen: On any Friday of Lent, said after Communion before a crucifix.
grants.partialWhen: On other days, said as a thanksgiving after Communion.

grants.title: Thanksgiving after Communion
grants.work: Making a thanksgiving after Communion with an approved prayer, such as the Soul of Christ (Anima Christi) or the prayer before a crucifix.
grants.partialWhen: When said as a thanksgiving after receiving Communion.

grants.title: Act of spiritual communion
grants.work: Making an act of spiritual communion in any approved form: telling Our Lord of your faith in his presence and your desire to receive him when you cannot receive him in the sacrament.
grants.partialWhen: Whenever it is made devoutly.

grants.title: Examination of conscience and act of contrition
grants.work: Examining your conscience with a resolve to amend, or making an act of contrition in any approved form, such as the Confiteor, Psalm 51 (Miserere), Psalm 130 (De profundis), or the gradual or penitential psalms. The Church mentions especially the time before confession, but the grant is not limited to it.
grants.partialWhen: Whenever it is done devoutly.

grants.title: A retreat of three days or more
grants.work: Giving yourself to spiritual exercises, a retreat, for at least three full days.
grants.plenaryWhen: When the retreat lasts at least three full days.

grants.title: Monthly recollection
grants.work: Taking part in a monthly day or hour of recollection.
grants.partialWhen: Each time you take part.

grants.title: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity
grants.work: Praying for the unity of Christians, for whom Christ prayed that all may be one.
grants.plenaryWhen: When you take part in several of the services held during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity and in its closing celebration.
grants.partialWhen: For an approved prayer for Christian unity at any time.

grants.title: At the hour of death
grants.work: A priest bringing the sacraments to someone in danger of death gives the apostolic blessing, which carries a plenary indulgence. If no priest can be had, the Church herself grants a plenary indulgence at the moment of death to anyone rightly disposed who has been in the habit of saying some prayers during life; in that case she supplies the three usual conditions. It is good to hold or look upon a crucifix or cross.
grants.plenaryWhen: At the point of death, even if a plenary indulgence has already been gained that day.

grants.title: Adoration of the Cross on Good Friday
grants.work: Taking part devoutly in the adoration of the Cross during the solemn liturgy of Good Friday.
grants.plenaryWhen: On Good Friday, at the celebration of the Lord’s Passion.

grants.title: The Way of the Cross
grants.work: Making the Stations of the Cross before stations lawfully set up, moving from one to the next and meditating on the Passion and death of the Lord. Fourteen stations are needed; meditation on the Passion as a whole is enough, without a separate reflection on each station. When it is made publicly and all cannot move, it is enough for the leader to go from station to station. Someone lawfully prevented from making it can gain the indulgence by reading and meditating on the Passion for some time, for example a quarter of an hour. Joining devoutly in the Way of the Cross led by the Pope, followed live by television or radio, also counts.
grants.plenaryWhen: On any day, when made as described.

grants.title: Using a blessed crucifix, rosary, scapular or medal
grants.work: Using with devotion a crucifix or cross, a rosary, a scapular or a medal that has been duly blessed by a priest or deacon.
grants.partialWhen: Whenever it is used with devotion.

grants.title: A blessed object on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul
grants.work: Using with devotion a crucifix, cross, rosary, scapular or medal blessed by the Pope or by any bishop, and adding a profession of faith in any approved form, such as the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul, 29 June.

grants.title: Mental prayer
grants.work: Giving yourself devoutly to mental prayer, silent prayer of the heart, for your own growth in the spiritual life.
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Hearing the word of God preached
grants.work: Listening attentively and devoutly to the preaching of the word of God.
grants.plenaryWhen: During a parish mission, when you have heard several of its sermons and take part in its solemn close.
grants.partialWhen: For attending other preaching of the word of God.

grants.title: The Rosary
grants.work: Praying five decades of the Rosary without a break, joining meditation on the mysteries to the spoken prayers. When it is said publicly the mysteries are announced in the usual way; when said privately it is enough to meditate on them as you pray.
grants.plenaryWhen: When it is prayed in a church or oratory, in a family, in a religious community or an association of the faithful, or wherever several people gather for a good purpose; or when you join devoutly in the Rosary led by the Pope and followed live by television or radio. On any day.
grants.partialWhen: In other circumstances, for example when prayed alone. If it is cut short for a good reason, the decades prayed carry a partial indulgence.

grants.title: Prayers to Our Lady
grants.work: Saying devoutly the Magnificat; the Angelus in the morning, at midday or in the evening, or in Eastertide the Regina Caeli, each with its versicles and prayer; or another approved prayer to Our Lady, such as the Memorare, the Hail, Holy Queen (Salve Regina), We fly to thy protection (Sub tuum praesidium), Maria, Mater gratiae or Sancta Maria, succurre miseris.
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Prayer to one’s guardian angel
grants.work: Calling devoutly on your guardian angel with an approved prayer, such as the Angel of God (Angele Dei).
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Prayer to Saint Joseph
grants.work: Calling devoutly on Saint Joseph, spouse of the Blessed Virgin, with an approved prayer, such as To thee, O blessed Joseph (Ad te, beate Ioseph).
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Prayer to Saints Peter and Paul
grants.work: Saying devoutly the prayer that begins “Holy Apostles Peter and Paul” (Sancti Apostoli Petre et Paule).
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Honouring the saint of the day
grants.work: On a saint’s day in the calendar, praying in his or her honour the prayer of the day from the Missal or another approved prayer.
grants.partialWhen: On the saint’s day.

grants.title: A newly canonised saint or newly beatified
grants.work: Visiting devoutly a church or oratory where celebrations are held, within the year, in honour of a new saint or blessed, and there saying the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: Once, for such a visit during that year of celebrations.
grants.partialWhen: For further devout visits in the same period.

grants.title: Novenas, litanies and little offices
grants.work: Taking part devoutly in a public novena, such as those before Christmas, Pentecost or the Immaculate Conception; saying an approved litany, such as those of the Holy Name, the Sacred Heart, the Precious Blood, Our Lady, Saint Joseph or the Saints; or saying an approved little office.
grants.partialWhen: Each time. A novena carries the indulgence when it is held publicly.

grants.title: The Akathistos and other prayers of the Eastern Churches
grants.work: Saying devoutly the Akathistos hymn or the office of the Paraclisis to the Mother of God (for the Akathistos, a suitable part said without a break is enough), or certain prayers of the Eastern traditions at their proper time.
grants.plenaryWhen: For the Akathistos or Paraclisis said in a church or oratory, in a family, in a religious community or association, or wherever several gather for a good purpose.
grants.partialWhen: In other circumstances, and for the other Eastern prayers named in the grant.

grants.title: Prayer for benefactors
grants.work: Out of gratitude before God, praying devoutly for your benefactors with an approved prayer, such as Retribuere dignare, Domine (“Vouchsafe, O Lord, to reward”).
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Prayer for the Pope and for one’s bishop
grants.work: Praying devoutly, as a son or daughter, an approved prayer for the Pope, such as Let us pray for our Pontiff (Oremus pro Pontifice); or praying the Missal’s prayer for your diocesan bishop at the beginning of his ministry or on its anniversary.
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Veni, Creator Spiritus
grants.work: Being present devoutly at the solemn singing or recitation of the hymn Come, Creator Spirit in a church or oratory, to ask God’s help.
grants.plenaryWhen: On 1 January, for the year ahead, and on the solemnity of Pentecost, at its solemn singing or recitation in a church or oratory.
grants.partialWhen: Said at other times, at the beginning or end of the day or of your work.

grants.title: Te Deum at the end of the year
grants.work: Being present devoutly at the solemn singing or recitation of the Te Deum in a church or oratory, to thank God for the blessings of the year.
grants.plenaryWhen: On 31 December, at its solemn singing or recitation in a church or oratory.
grants.partialWhen: Said at other times, at the beginning or end of the day or of your work.

grants.title: Prayers at the turning points of the day
grants.work: Saying devoutly an approved prayer of petition or thanksgiving at the beginning and end of the day, at the beginning and end of your work, and before and after meals. The Church names, among others, grace before meals (Benedic, Domine), grace after meals (Agimus tibi gratias), Visit this house (Visita, quaesumus), Come, Holy Spirit (Veni, Sancte Spiritus), Actiones nostras, the Te Deum and the Veni Creator.
grants.partialWhen: At those moments of the day.

grants.title: A priest’s first Mass
grants.work: A newly ordained priest celebrating his first Mass with the people on an appointed day, and the faithful who devoutly attend it.
grants.plenaryWhen: At that Mass.

grants.title: Jubilees of ordination
grants.work: A priest on the 25th, 50th, 60th or 70th anniversary of his ordination, or a bishop on the 25th, 40th or 50th anniversary of his, renewing before God his resolve to be faithful to the duties of his calling; and the faithful who devoutly attend the jubilee Mass.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the jubilee, at the jubilee Mass.

grants.title: Renewal of baptismal promises
grants.work: Renewing the promises of your baptism in any approved form: renouncing sin and Satan and professing the faith.
grants.plenaryWhen: At the Easter Vigil, and on the anniversary of your own baptism.
grants.partialWhen: At any other time.

grants.title: The sign of the cross, the Creed, and the acts of faith, hope and love
grants.work: Making the sign of the cross devoutly with its words, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; saying the Apostles’ Creed or the Nicene Creed; or making an act of faith, hope or charity in any approved form.
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Visiting a cemetery for the dead
grants.work: Visiting a cemetery devoutly and praying for the dead there, even only in your mind. This indulgence can be offered only for the souls in purgatory.
grants.plenaryWhen: On each day from 1 to 8 November.
grants.partialWhen: On any other day of the year.

grants.title: A church visit for All Souls
grants.work: Visiting a church or oratory devoutly and saying there the Our Father and the Creed, for the souls in purgatory. With the diocesan bishop’s consent this may be done instead on the Sunday before or after, or on All Saints.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, 2 November. The visit may be made from noon on 1 November until midnight on 2 November.

grants.title: Prayers for the dead
grants.work: Saying devoutly Lauds or Vespers of the Office of the Dead, or the prayer Eternal rest (Requiem aeternam). This indulgence can be offered only for the souls in purgatory.
grants.partialWhen: Each time.

grants.title: Reading Holy Scripture
grants.work: Reading Holy Scripture in an edition approved by the Church, with the reverence due to the word of God and as spiritual reading. If you cannot read for a good reason, you may listen while someone reads it aloud, or by a recording.
grants.plenaryWhen: On any day, when you read or listen for at least half an hour.
grants.partialWhen: For a shorter time.

grants.title: A diocesan synod
grants.work: During a diocesan synod, visiting devoutly the church where it is being held and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: Once, during the synod.

grants.title: The bishop’s pastoral visitation
grants.work: During a pastoral visitation of your parish, attending a liturgy at which the bishop or his delegate presides.
grants.plenaryWhen: Once, during the visitation.

grants.title: A visit to your parish church
grants.work: Visiting your parish church devoutly and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the parish’s titular feast and on 2 August, the day of the Portiuncula indulgence, the Pardon of Assisi.

grants.title: A visit to the cathedral
grants.work: Visiting a cathedral devoutly and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul (29 June), on the cathedral’s titular feast, on the Chair of Saint Peter (22 February), on the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica (9 November), and on 2 August, the Portiuncula.

grants.title: A visit to a minor basilica
grants.work: Visiting a minor basilica devoutly and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul (29 June), on the basilica’s titular feast, on 2 August (the Portiuncula), and once a year on a day of your choosing.

grants.title: A visit to a shrine
grants.work: Visiting devoutly a shrine recognised by the Church, international, national or diocesan, and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the shrine’s titular feast, once a year on a day of your choosing, and whenever you go there with a group on pilgrimage.

grants.title: A church on the day of its dedication
grants.work: Visiting devoutly a church, or an altar, on the anniversary of its dedication, and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the day of the church’s or altar’s dedication.

grants.title: A religious church on its founder’s feast
grants.work: Visiting devoutly a church or oratory of a religious order or congregation, or of a society of apostolic life, and saying there the Our Father and the Creed.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the feast of the order’s holy founder.

grants.title: The papal basilicas, stational churches and catacombs of Rome
grants.work: Visiting one of the four papal basilicas of Rome, making the visit as a pilgrimage with others or at least expressing there a son’s or daughter’s loyalty to the Pope, and saying the Our Father and the Creed; taking part in the liturgy at a stational church on its own day; or visiting a catacomb or ancient Christian cemetery.
grants.plenaryWhen: At a papal basilica on any day; at a stational church when you take part in its liturgy on its day.
grants.partialWhen: For another devout visit to a stational church, and for a devout visit to a catacomb.

grants.title: Divine Mercy Sunday
grants.work: In any church or chapel, with a heart wholly detached from sin, even venial sin, taking part in prayers and devotions in honour of the Divine Mercy; or, before the Blessed Sacrament, exposed or in the tabernacle, saying the Our Father and the Creed and adding a devout prayer to the merciful Lord Jesus, such as “Merciful Jesus, I trust in you”. Those who cannot go to church, such as the sick, those who care for them, sailors at sea, people driven from home by war and those with a just reason to stay home, may say the Our Father and the Creed before an image of the merciful Jesus with a prayer to him; and if even that is impossible, unite themselves in spirit with those who are praying, offering their sufferings, with the intention of meeting the usual conditions as soon as they can.
grants.plenaryWhen: On the Second Sunday of Easter, Divine Mercy Sunday, with the usual conditions.
grants.partialWhen: At any time, for praying to the merciful Lord Jesus with a contrite heart in an approved invocation.
grants.source: Apostolic Penitentiary, Decree on indulgences attached to devotions in honour of the Divine Mercy (2002)

misunderstandings.title: An indulgence does not forgive sin.
misunderstandings.text: Sin is forgiven by God when we repent, and grave sin through confession. An indulgence touches only what remains after a sin has been forgiven. It is never permission to sin, and it does not replace confession or the Mass, which the Church places far above it.

misunderstandings.title: No “days” or “years” any more.
misunderstandings.text: Old prayer cards that promise “300 days” or “seven years” use a measure Pope Paul VI abolished in 1967. Today an indulgence is simply partial or plenary. The old collections of indulgenced prayers were replaced by the Church’s present list, the Enchiridion Indulgentiarum, so a grant printed in an old prayer book may no longer stand.

misunderstandings.title: No indulgence for chain prayers or printed promises.
misunderstandings.text: Indulgences come only from the Church’s own grants, made by the Pope through the Apostolic Penitentiary or by bishops within the limits of the law. Nothing is gained by passing a prayer on, by making a set number of copies, or by saying a prayer that a leaflet says “never fails”. Such promises are not the Church’s.

misunderstandings.title: An indulgence cannot be bought.
misunderstandings.text: The Church has condemned the old abuses, money-making among them. An alms given to the poor can be a good work of charity, and the Church sometimes counts such charity among the works she asks for, but nothing given ever purchases a grace.

misunderstandings.title: No one can guarantee the release of a particular soul.
misunderstandings.text: An indulgence offered for the dead is offered as a prayer of intercession, by way of suffrage, and its effect rests with God’s mercy. It is a real help to the souls in purgatory, and a work of love worth doing, but no one can promise that a named person has been set free by it.

misunderstandings.title: A plenary indulgence does not need perfect feelings.
misunderstandings.text: Freedom from attachment to sin is a matter of the will: sincerely wanting no sin at all. Temptations, distractions and a dry heart do not prevent it. If your detachment falls short, the indulgence is partial, not lost. There is no need to examine yourself anxiously about whether you gained it; do what the Church asks with a sincere heart and leave the rest to God.

misunderstandings.title: Not attached to things or places by themselves.
misunderstandings.text: Even when an indulgence is tied to a blessed object or a church, it is granted for what a person does there with faith: the devout use, the visit, the prayer. A medal or a building does not carry it by itself.

special.title: The Year of Saint Francis
special.text: For the eighth centenary of the death of Saint Francis of Assisi (3 October 1226), the Church keeps a special year from 10 January 2026 to 10 January 2027. A plenary indulgence may be gained by going on pilgrimage to any Franciscan conventual church, or to any church anywhere in the world dedicated to Saint Francis or connected with him, and there taking part in the celebrations of the year or spending a fitting time in prayer and meditation, asking for charity towards one’s neighbour and for peace among peoples, and ending with the Our Father, the Creed and prayers to Our Lady, Saint Francis, Saint Clare and the saints of the Franciscan family. The usual conditions apply, with a heart detached from sin, and the indulgence may be offered for the dead. The elderly, the sick, those who care for them and anyone who cannot leave home for a serious reason may gain it by uniting themselves in spirit with the celebrations and offering their prayers and sufferings to God, intending to meet the usual conditions as soon as they can.
special.source: Apostolic Penitentiary, Decree for the eighth centenary of the death of Saint Francis of Assisi, 10 January 2026
