about: The Church fasts because the Lord asks for a change of heart. “Rend your hearts, and not your garments,” says the prophet Joel, and Jesus tells us to fast in secret, for the Father who sees in secret. The Church teaches that the call to penance does not aim first at outward works but at interior conversion. Without that, fasting is empty; with it, fasting becomes its sign and its help. (Joel 2:13; Matthew 6:16-18; Catechism 1430.)

Fasting never stands alone. Scripture and the Fathers join it to prayer and almsgiving, which turn us towards God and towards our neighbour, and Isaiah names the fast that God has chosen: to loose the bands of wickedness and to deal bread to the hungry. What we go without is meant to make room for God and to reach those who have less. (Catechism 1434; Paenitemini; Isaiah 58:6-7.)

Saint Paul VI wrote that penance is lived first in faithfulness to the duties of one’s state of life, in accepting the difficulties of work and of living with others, and in bearing the trials of each day with patience. The days of fasting and abstinence the Church sets are few and light. They are meant to give us mastery over ourselves and freedom of heart, not to weigh on us, and no one is asked to harm their health to keep them. (Paenitemini; Catechism 2043.)
interior: Penance begins in the heart: God asks first that we turn back to him, and fasting is the sign and the help of that turning, not a substitute for it.
Its surest form is the day you already have: your duties done faithfully, the difficulties of work and of other people accepted, and the trials of the day borne with patience.
Fasting belongs with prayer and charity: what we go without makes room for God and is meant to reach those who have less.

law.title: Everyone is called to penance
law.text: By God’s law every Christian is to do penance, each in his or her own way. So that we do it together, the Church sets common days for prayer, works of piety and charity, doing our duties more faithfully, and above all fasting and abstinence.

law.title: Fridays and Lent
law.text: The Church’s days and season of penance are every Friday of the year and the whole of Lent.

law.title: Abstinence on Fridays
law.text: On every Friday the Church’s rule is abstinence from meat, or from another food named by the bishops’ conference, unless a solemnity falls on that Friday. A bishops’ conference may allow another penance in its place, so the practice outside Lent differs from country to country.

law.title: Who is bound
law.text: Abstinence from meat binds from the 14th birthday, for life. Fasting binds from the 18th birthday until the 59th birthday (the beginning of the sixtieth year, as the law puts it).
law.source: Code of Canon Law, can. 1252 with can. 97

law.title: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday
law.text: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of both fasting and abstinence from meat, everywhere. They are the only two days of the year on which fasting is required.
law.who: Abstinence: from the 14th birthday. Fasting: from the 18th birthday until the 59th birthday.

law.title: Children and the young
law.text: Those too young to be bound are not asked to fast or abstain, but parents and pastors are to teach them what penance truly means.

law.title: Bishops’ conferences
law.text: Each bishops’ conference may set the details, and may replace fasting and abstinence, wholly or in part, with other penances, especially works of charity and of piety.

law.title: When you cannot
law.text: For a good reason, a parish priest can excuse a person from a day of penance in a particular case, or change it into another good work. It is better to ask than to worry.

law.title: Eastern Catholics
law.text: Eastern Catholics keep the fasts of their own Church, which differ from these.
law.who: Members of the Eastern Catholic Churches

us.title: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday
us.text: On Ash Wednesday and Good Friday both fasting and abstinence from meat are required. These are the only two fast days of the year.
us.source: US bishops, Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence (1966), 12; USCCB, Fast and Abstinence

us.title: The Fridays of Lent
us.text: Every Friday of Lent is a day of abstinence from meat for everyone from the 14th birthday. If a solemnity falls on a Friday of Lent, such as Saint Joseph on 19 March or the Annunciation on 25 March, abstinence is lifted that day.
us.source: Pastoral Statement (1966), 13; Code of Canon Law, can. 1251; USCCB, Fast and Abstinence

us.title: Fridays through the year
us.text: Outside Lent, Friday is still a day of penance. The bishops no longer require abstinence from meat on these Fridays, but they put it first among the penances they suggest, and hope people will keep it freely. You may choose another penance instead, such as a work of charity, time given to prayer, or going without something you enjoy. Those who abstain should not judge those who choose otherwise.
us.source: Pastoral Statement (1966), 22-26, kept in force by the USCCB complementary norm to cann. 1252-1253 (1983)

us.title: What fasting means
us.text: On a fast day you may eat one full meal. Two smaller meals are allowed if you need them, but together they should be less than a full meal. Nothing solid between meals; drinks are allowed at any time.
us.source: USCCB, Fast and Abstinence; USCCB, Questions and Answers about Lent

us.title: What abstinence means
us.text: Abstinence means no meat from animals that live on land, such as beef, pork, lamb and chicken; birds count as meat. Fish, shellfish and other cold-blooded animals are allowed, and so are eggs, milk, cheese and butter. Broth and gravy made from meat are not forbidden, though many leave them aside in the spirit of the day. A lavish seafood dinner keeps the letter and misses the point.
us.source: USCCB, Questions and Answers about Lent; Paul VI, Paenitemini (1966), norm III

us.title: Who is excused
us.text: Beyond the age limits, those excused include the physically or mentally ill, among them people with long-term illnesses such as diabetes, and women who are pregnant or nursing. Common sense should rule, and no one who is ill should put their health at further risk by fasting. The frail, those whose work is heavy, and guests who cannot refuse without giving offence have also traditionally been excused, as far as need requires.
us.source: USCCB, Questions and Answers about Lent; for the last sentence, C. B. Donovan, EWTN, Fast and Abstinence (secondary)

us.title: Sundays
us.text: Sundays, even in Lent, are not days of fasting or abstinence. Whether you keep your own Lenten sacrifice on Sundays is left to your conscience.
us.source: USCCB, Questions and Answers about Lent

us.title: If you never eat meat
us.text: If you never eat meat, you already keep abstinence. You may choose another small penance if you wish; it is not required.
us.source: J. M. Cooper, JCL, OSV News column, March 2025 (secondary)

eucharistic.title: Before Holy Communion
eucharistic.text: Whoever is to receive Holy Communion takes no food or drink for at least one hour beforehand, except water and medicine. The hour is counted to the moment of Communion, not to the start of Mass, though many find it simpler to begin an hour before Mass. A priest who celebrates two or three Masses in a day may eat between them.
eucharistic.excused: The elderly, the sick, and those who care for them may receive Communion even if they have eaten within the hour.
eucharistic.source: Code of Canon Law, can. 919; on counting the hour, A. Strouse, Adoremus, 11 May 2025 (secondary)

voluntary.title: Wednesday
voluntary.when: Every Wednesday, except solemnities, Ash Wednesday (already a fast day) and the octaves of Christmas and Easter
voluntary.text: The Didache, an early Christian handbook, tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays: “do ye keep your fast on the fourth and on the preparation (the sixth) day.” Saint Francis de Sales mentions the custom and leaves it to each person’s devotion and the advice of a director. No law asks it today; it is a free offering.
voluntary.source: Didache 8.1, tr. J. B. Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers (London, 1891); Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life III.23

voluntary.title: Weekdays of Lent
voluntary.when: Monday to Thursday and Saturday in Lent, from the Thursday after Ash Wednesday to the Wednesday of Holy Week, except solemnities
voluntary.text: The US bishops strongly recommend a fast of your own choosing on the weekdays of Lent, together with daily Mass where you can, generosity to those in need, Scripture, the Stations and the Rosary. It is a recommendation, not a law: choose what fits your state of life and your health.

voluntary.title: The paschal fast
voluntary.when: Holy Saturday, until the Easter Vigil
voluntary.text: The Second Vatican Council asks that the paschal fast of Good Friday be prolonged, where possible, through Holy Saturday until the Easter Vigil, so that we come to the joy of Easter with an uplifted and clear mind. It is recommended, not required.
voluntary.source: Sacrosanctum Concilium 110; General Norms for the Liturgical Year 20; USCCB, Fast and Abstinence

voluntary.title: Ember days
voluntary.when: The Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after the first Sunday of Lent, after Pentecost Sunday, after the third Sunday of September, and after 13 December (the third week of Advent), as the 1962 books keep them; before 1960 the September days followed 14 September
voluntary.text: Four times a year, with the seasons, the Church in Rome kept three days of fasting and prayer, and ordinations were often held on the Saturday. They no longer bind. The Church still keeps such days for prayer for the needs of all people, for the fruits of the earth and for human work, and for thanksgiving, and leaves their arrangement to the bishops. Some keep them with a fast, freely.
voluntary.source: General Norms for the Liturgical Year (1969) 45-47; Pastoral Statement (1966), 17; history and dates: Wikipedia, “Ember days” (secondary)

voluntary.title: The eve of a great feast
voluntary.when: The day before Christmas, Pentecost, the Assumption, All Saints and the Immaculate Conception (24 December, the Saturday before Pentecost, 14 August, 31 October, 7 December), unless that day is a Sunday or a solemnity
voluntary.text: These eves were once days of fasting. No law asks it now, but the US bishops suggest that the devout may freely prepare for the Church’s feasts with a day of particular self-denial and prayer, as in the old saying, a fast before a feast.
voluntary.source: Pastoral Statement (1966), 17; former vigils: Wikipedia, ’Fasting and abstinence in the Catholic Church’ (secondary)

voluntary.title: Saturday, for Our Lady
voluntary.when: Saturdays, except solemnities, Holy Saturday and the octaves of Christmas and Easter
voluntary.text: The Roman calendar allows a memorial of Our Lady on Saturdays in Ordinary Time when no other memorial falls, and many keep Saturday in her honour. Some offer a small self-denial on Saturday through her. It is a devotion, freely chosen.
voluntary.source: General Norms for the Liturgical Year 15; Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life III.23

voluntary.title: Advent
voluntary.text: Advent is a season of devout and joyful expectation, not a season of required fasting. In earlier centuries it had a penitential character, and the US bishops praise those who keep something of that spirit. Any self-denial you choose is your own.
voluntary.source: General Norms for the Liturgical Year 39; Pastoral Statement (1966), 4-6; Code of Canon Law, can. 1250

voluntary.title: Going without something good
voluntary.text: Freely going without something good that you enjoy, in a spirit of penance, carries a partial indulgence. It is best joined to charity: give to someone in need what the sacrifice saves.
voluntary.source: Enchiridion Indulgentiarum (1999), third general grant; Catechism 1434, 1438

health: No one is asked to harm their health by fasting. The sick, including those with long-term illnesses such as diabetes, the mentally ill, and women who are pregnant or nursing are excused.

If you are unsure whether your health allows it, ask your doctor; if you are unsure what the Church asks of you, ask a priest. A parish priest can excuse you, or change the obligation into another good work.

If you have, or are recovering from, an eating disorder, food rules of any kind can do harm. Speak with your doctor or care team and with a priest before keeping any fast. The Church excuses those who are ill, and prayer and works of charity remain open to you.
Penance is about conversion of heart and love of neighbour. It is not a diet, and it is never about weight, appearance or punishing yourself.
If fasting begins to feel like control, or leaves you anxious or ashamed, stop, and speak to someone you trust.
Saint Francis de Sales advised against long and immoderate fasting, especially for the young, and counselled taking on no bodily austerities without the advice of a spiritual guide.
If you forget a day of abstinence, or could not keep it, do not be troubled. Begin again in peace; a priest can help if it weighs on you.
Those below the ages of the law are not asked to fast. They can learn what penance means through small acts of kindness and self-denial.

countries.text: Since 16 September 2011 the bishops ask all Catholics who are able to abstain from meat on every Friday of the year.
countries.source: Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales, Friday Penance (May 2011), as reported by Wikipedia; the statement itself was not opened

countries.text: The bishops ask for a penance every Friday and suggest, among other things, abstaining from meat or alcohol.
countries.source: Irish Catholic Bishops’ Conference, Friday Penance (2010), as reported by Wikipedia

countries.text: Fridays are days of abstinence, but acts of charity or piety may take its place.
countries.source: Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, Keeping Friday (2006), as reported by Wikipedia

countries.text: Abstinence on Fridays is not obligatory, provided another form of penance is kept. Ash Wednesday and Good Friday remain days of fasting and abstinence.
countries.source: Australian Catholic Bishops’ Conference, complementary legislation (1985), as reported by Wikipedia; Code of Canon Law, can. 1251

countries.text: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence everywhere. For the other Fridays, follow your own bishops’ conference.
Follow the fasts of your own Church.
